Wailing and Gnashing of Teeth
WAY-ling and NASHA-ing uv TEETH
n. phrase (eschatological; the phrase used seven times by Jesus in the Gospels to describe the sensory experience of hell — weeping, anguish, and uncontrollable rage in eternal outer darkness)
Wail from Old Norse væla (to lament, moan); a sustained, loud cry of grief or pain. Gnash from Middle English gnasten, probably from Old Norse gnastan (a gnashing sound); to grind or clash the teeth in rage or agony. The combination captures two dimensions of the condemned: grief over what is lost (weeping) and furious, helpless rage against God's judgment (gnashing) — both without end, without relief, and without hope.

Biblical Definition

Jesus uses the phrase “weeping and gnashing of teeth” seven times in the Gospel of Matthew (8:12; 13:42, 50; 22:13; 24:51; 25:30) and once in Luke (13:28). Each occurrence describes the experiential reality of hell for those condemned in the final judgment. The imagery is deliberately sensory: weeping (grief, anguish, loss) and gnashing of teeth (rage, torment, fury). Matthew 8:12 sets it in the context of unbelieving Israel excluded from the messianic feast: “the sons of the kingdom shall be cast out into the outer darkness; in that place there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” The “outer darkness” motif recurs in Matthew 22:13 (the man without a wedding garment) and 25:30 (the worthless slave), positioning the condemned outside the feast's light and warmth in an exclusion that is total, perpetual, and irreversible. Matthew 13:42 locates the weeping and gnashing in the “furnace of fire,” combining heat and darkness as complementary dimensions of the same reality. The phrase is not merely rhetorical intensification; it is the Lord Jesus Christ's own testimony about the character of eternal condemnation — experiential, conscious, and unending. The 1689 LBCF (32.2) and Westminster Confession (32.2) affirm that the wicked will be “cast into eternal torments.” The phrase is Jesus' sobering gift to the church: He who knows the Father also knows the cost of final separation from Him.

Webster 1828 Definition

The sevenfold Gospel phrase describing the experiential character of hell — weeping in grief and gnashing teeth in fury — used by Jesus himself to testify to the reality of eternal, conscious torment for the condemned; a central element of the Lord's eschatological warning.

WAILING AND GNASHING OF TEETH, n. phrase. The sensory description of hell used seven times by Jesus in the Synoptic Gospels — five times in Matthew alone — to characterize the experiential state of those condemned in the final judgment. The phrase consistently accompanies the language of “outer darkness,” “the furnace of fire,” and exclusion from the messianic feast, situating the condemned in a state of total deprivation from the light, warmth, and joy of God's presence.

The two elements of the phrase are complementary and revealing: weeping (klauthmos, loud, sustained lamentation) names the grief of irretrievable loss — the realization, too late, of what was squandered; gnashing of teeth (brugmos, grinding or clashing of teeth) names the rage that has no object capable of receiving it — the fury of the condemned turned inward or directed at a God now completely beyond reach. These are not the emotions of purgatorial correction; they are the permanent posture of those for whom no correction remains possible.

The phrase appears in Matthew 8:12 (unbelieving sons of the kingdom cast out), 13:42 (the tares cast into the furnace), 13:50 (the bad fish cast out), 22:13 (the man without a wedding garment cast into outer darkness), 24:51 (the hypocritical servant cut in two), 25:30 (the worthless slave cast into outer darkness), and Luke 13:28 (those excluded from the kingdom seeing Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and the prophets within). The variety of parables and contexts demonstrates that the phrase is not attached to a single type of sinner; it is Jesus' standard description of the experiential state of all the condemned.

Reformed confessional theology follows the Lord's lead: Westminster Confession 32.2 and 1689 LBCF 32.2 both affirm that the wicked will be raised to dishonor and “cast into eternal torments.” Annihilationism, which holds the condemned are extinguished rather than tormented, cannot account for the experiential language of weeping and gnashing: both require a conscious, experiencing subject. The existence of the torment without the subject who suffers it is incoherent.

The homiletic purpose of the phrase is unmistakable: Jesus employs it not to satisfy curiosity about the afterlife but to warn His hearers of what awaits the impenitent and to press the urgency of faith and repentance. It is the negative side of the gospel's double-sided proclamation: the same Christ who says “Come to Me, all who are weary” (Matt 11:28) also says there is a place where the weeping never stops and the teeth never unclench.

Key Scripture

Matthew 8:12 — "But the children of the kingdom shall be cast out into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Matthew 22:13 — "Then said the king to the servants, Bind him hand and foot, and take him away, and cast him into outer darkness; there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Matthew 13:42 — "And shall cast them into a furnace of fire: there shall be wailing and gnashing of teeth."

Matthew 25:30 — "And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth."

Modern Corruption

Liberal theology and the emergent church tradition read the phrase as hyperbolic Semitic idiom for emphatic warning rather than literal eschatological description; annihilationism denies the experiential continuity the phrase requires by holding the condemned are extinguished before the weeping begins.

expand to see more

The most common liberal theological move against the wailing-and-gnashing phrase is to classify it as hyperbolic Semitic idiom — intense language used by first-century Jewish teachers to press urgency but not intended as literal description of afterlife experience. This reading is associated with Edward Fudge, Clark Pinnock, and the annihilationist tradition, and more broadly with the progressive dismantling of the traditional hell doctrine across mainline Protestantism and the emergent church movement. The problem is that the phrase consistently accompanies concrete spatial language (“outer darkness,” “furnace of fire,” “Gehenna”) in contexts where Jesus is giving serious warning rather than casual figure — and that dismissing the language as “mere idiom” tends to apply only when the text is inconvenient, not as a consistent hermeneutical principle. Jesus' audience, shaped by Jewish Second Temple eschatology, would not have heard “weeping and gnashing of teeth” as a comfortable metaphor.

Annihilationism (the view that the condemned are eventually extinguished, ceasing to exist) faces an internal problem with this phrase: weeping requires a subject who weeps; gnashing requires teeth that gnash. If the condemned cease to exist, the experiential language is meaningless, not merely symbolic. Revelation 14:11 reinforces the continuity: “the smoke of their torment rises forever and ever, and they have no rest, day or night.” The phrase “they have no rest” presupposes continuous experience by a continuous subject. Reformed confessional theology, following the plain reading of Jesus' own words, affirms eternal, conscious torment as the state of the condemned — not because it is a pleasant doctrine but because it is what the Lord taught, and the teacher is trustworthy.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The phrase is rooted in the Synoptic tradition of Jesus' eschatological teaching, the Second Temple Jewish conception of Gehenna, the Old Testament prophetic imagery of divine wrath, and the Reformed confessional doctrine of eternal punishment.

expand to see more

Synoptic eschatological discourse — the seven occurrences in Matthew and Luke cluster around the final judgment parables (tares, dragnet, wedding feast, servants, talents) and the Olivet Discourse; the phrase is Jesus' consistent idiom for the condemned's experiential state.

Second Temple Jewish Gehenna imagery — the Valley of Hinnom (Ge-Hinnom, Gehenna) south of Jerusalem was the city's burning rubbish pit and the site of child sacrifice under Molech; it became the primary metaphor for the place of punishment; Jesus' “outer darkness” and “furnace of fire” add to this tradition without replacing it.

Isaiah 66:24 / Mark 9:47–48 — “their worm does not die, and the fire is not quenched”; the Old Testament prophetic foundation for the unending character of the condemnation; quoted by Jesus three times in Mark 9 as the description of Gehenna.

Westminster Confession 32.2 / 1689 LBCF 32.2 — the condemned raised “to dishonor and everlasting contempt”; the confessional commitment to conscious, eternal punishment grounded in the same biblical texts Jesus cites.

Westminster Larger Catechism Q. 29 — “What are the punishments of sin in the world to come?” — “everlasting separation from the comfortable presence of God, and most grievous torments in soul and body, without intermission, in hell fire for ever” — the confessional unpacking of weeping and gnashing.

Usage

"The sevenfold repetition of the phrase across multiple parables is not accidental; Jesus uses the same phrase to describe the fate of the excluded Israelite (8:12), the apostate servant (24:51), and the unprofitable servant (25:30) — demonstrating that no particular category of sinner escapes the description; the warning is catholic."

"The weeping and the gnashing are not the same: weeping suggests grief over what is lost (the feasting, the fellowship, the presence of God); gnashing suggests fury at what cannot be undone — together they capture the complete emotional landscape of a soul that knows exactly what it forfeited and cannot recover it."

"Pastors who avoid preaching on this phrase rob their congregations of the urgency Jesus built into His gospel proclamation: He who invited all to the feast (Matt 11:28) also warned in the starkest terms what awaits those who decline the invitation — the outer darkness, the furnace, the unending grief."
